title: Operation Tidal Wave in Boston Leads to 87 Cruise Ship Crew Removals by CBP for Child Sexual Exploitation Materials
body: BOSTON — U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers at the Port of Boston have now removed 87 aliens from cruise ships as part of the ongoing "Operation Tidal Wave" initiative, a multi-agency effort targeting the possession and distribution of child sexual abuse material and child sexual exploitation material among cruise ship crewmembers. This milestone follows the most recent enforcement action on Sept. 20 where officers removed six additional crewmembers from the cruise ship Breakaway . On Sept. 20, CBP officers encountered six citizens of the Philippines aboard the Breakaway . During secondary interviews at Boston Logan International Airport, all six subjects admitted to previously possessing CSEM/CSAM. Following comprehensive searches of their living quarters and electronic devices, all six were processed for removal of conditional landing under Section 212(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) of the Immigration and Nationality Act for crimes involving moral turpitude. "The success of Operation Tidal Wave reflects the unwavering dedication of our officers and partners to protect the most vulnerable," said Acting Director of Field Operations Julio Caravia. "Let the removal of these 87 be a message to others: we will not accept this exploitation and CBP will not stop identifying and arresting the individuals who participate in it." This mission builds upon the success of previous phases of Operation Tidal Wave conducted across the United States. Earlier this year, Phase 1 in San Diego (April) resulted in administrative enforcement actions against 27 crewmembers from six vessels, while Phase 2 in San Juan (June/July) led to the removal of 14 crewmembers and the acceptance of federal prosecution for one individual. In the Boston area, these efforts have been consistent throughout the summer, resulting in the removal of 87 crew members from various vessels since mid-August. Operation Tidal Wave is a multiagency initiative led by the CBP Office of Field Operations Enforcement Operations Division, in coordination with Homeland Security Investigations and the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force. The operation aims to identify and initiate enforcement actions against cruise ship crewmembers who, based on intelligence, are associated with the possession, use, procurement, production, or distribution of CSEM and CSAM. The Area Port of Boston plans to continue this operational effort through the remainder of the fiscal year. This initiative demonstrates effective coordination among CBP field elements, targeting units, and HSI to address CSAM-related concerns within the cruise vessel crewmember population. CBP remains committed to working with domestic and international partners to identify and interdict those who pose a threat to public safety and to prevent the exploitation of children. Under federal law, any involvement with CSEM is strictly prohibited and carries severe penalties, including criminal prosecution, removal, and 10-year inadmissibility to the United States. title: New York man arrested after CBP officers seize 65 pounds of khat in passenger baggage at Dulles Airport
body: STERLING, Va. – A New York City man is facing felony drug charges after U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers discovered 65 pounds of khat ( Catha edulis ) in his baggage on Wednesday night at Washington Dulles International Airport. Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority Police arrested Bakari Wally, 24, a U.S. citizen from the Bronx, Thursday morning and charged him with possession with the intent to distribute and transporting a controlled substance into the Commonwealth of Virginia. CBP officer discovered 65 pounds of khat in a New York man's baggage. CBP officers referred Wally to a secondary examination after he arrived from Casablanca, Morocco, and discovered bags of a dried organic substance in his checked baggage. Field tests identified the organic substance as khat. The khat weighed 29.6 kilograms, or 65 pounds, four ounces. It has a street value of about $8,000. CBP officers seized the khat and turned Wally over to MWAA Police officers. “Travelers who smuggle illegal products to the United States will quickly learn that Customs and Border Protection will find it and we will work with our law enforcement partners to pursue severe consequences, including felony criminal charges as this traveler is facing,” said CBP Area Port Director Christine Waugh, Area Port of Washington, D.C. “Smugglers should know that the risk of prison time is not worth what transnational criminal organizations pay them to violate our nation’s laws.” Khat, known as Abyssinian tea and African salad, is typically grown in East Africa and the Arabian Peninsula and is chewed for its amphetamine-like effect. Users also boil dried khat leaves to create a stimulant tea. According to the DEA, khat contains two central nervous system stimulants -- cathinone, which is classified as a Schedule I controlled substance, and cathine, a Schedule IV controlled substance. Symptoms of khat toxicity include delusions, loss of appetite, difficulty breathing, and increased blood pressure and heart rate. The World Health Organization classified khat as a drug of abuse in 1980. CBP officers have observed an increase in khat being smuggled in traveler baggage. On Aug. 20, CBP officers seized 764 pounds on khat in the baggage of two men and on Aug. 14 seized 368 pounds of khat in another man’s baggage at Dulles airport. CBP officers also seized 412 pounds of khat and 847 pounds of khat in separate seizures in August at Baltimore Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport. CBP officers and agents seized about 46,000 pounds of khat last fiscal year (Oct. 1, 2024, through Sept. 30, 2025) and seized over 30,000 pounds of khat so far during the first 10 months of this fiscal year (Oct. 1, 2025, through Aug. 31, 2026). Every day, CBP officers and agents seized an average of about 1,600 pounds of dangerous drugs last year at and between our nation’s air, sea, and land ports of entry. title: CBP announces voluntary Electronic Export Manifest for truck cargo test
body: WASHINGTON — U.S. Customs and Border Protection is seeking test participants for a new voluntary test program — the Automated Commercial Environment Electronic Export Manifest for Truck Cargo Test. This initiative is designed to modernize trade processes, enhance cargo security, and improve the efficiency of export operations across U.S. borders. The test will evaluate the feasibility of requiring truck carriers to submit export manifest data electronically through ACE. By streamlining the collection of this data, CBP aims to better identify high-risk shipments, facilitate the movement of legitimate trade, and ensure compliance with U.S. export laws. Test Procedures: Participants in this voluntary test will agree to submit specific, limited export manifest data electronically to ACE at least 24 hours prior to departure from the United States. This initial submission will be complemented by a complete export manifest filing no later than two hours prior to arrival at the final port of export. This process allows CBP to link Electronic Export Information submitted by the U.S. Principal Party in Interest with the export manifest, enabling more effective risk assessment and targeted inspections prior to the loading of cargo. Participation and Eligibility: CBP is limiting this test to nine truck carriers. There are no restrictions regarding organization size, location, or commodity type; however, prospective participants must possess the technical capability to submit data electronically to CBP through ACE. Benefits of Participation: Participants in the test may experience several advantages, including: Reduced Costs – Fewer examinations required after cargo is loaded. Improved Efficiency – A reduction in delays and costs associated with border inspections. Enhanced Security – Leveraging CBP’s risk-based approach to improve cargo security and ensure compliance. Corporate Preparedness – Early insight into future mandatory electronic export manifest requirements. Duration: The test will run for approximately two years, beginning 30 days after the official publication of the notice in the Federal Register. CBP will evaluate the results throughout the duration of the test to determine if it should be extended, expanded, or modified. Interested parties may apply by submitting an email to cbptruckexportmanifest@cbp.dhs.gov . The email must state the applicant’s interest and qualifications, include a point of contact name and telephone number, and use the subject line: “Electronic Export Manifest for Truck Cargo Test Application.” Applications will be accepted until nine qualified parties have been selected. For more information on ACE, please visit the ACE: The Import and Export Processing System webpage. title: U.S. Border Patrol agents rescue four from locked train car
body: Fourth recent incident at same rural rail siding DEL RIO, Texas – For the fourth time in recent weeks, Del Rio Sector Border Patrol agents encountered illegal aliens who had been locked inside a freight car by smugglers. Agents rescue four from locked freight car. Uvalde Border Patrol Station agents made the discovery just before dawn on Sept. 16 while conducting an inspection of a stationary freight train on a rail siding near Knippa. A Border Patrol canine alerted agents to an autorack car carrying automobiles. Inside the freight car agents found four individuals locked inside with no means of escape. The individuals, three Mexican nationals and one Chinese national were transported to the Uvalde Station for processing. The rescue marks the fourth such incident involving autorack freight train cars within a three-week span at the same railroad siding. On Sept. 11, agents found two individuals locked in an autorack car, one of whom was deceased. Homeland Security Investigations is investigating that incident. Freight cars pose extreme danger to migrants. On Sept. 7, agents rescued three individuals from an autorack car hauler at the same rail siding. That event followed the Aug. 30 rescue of eight individuals, including one child, under identical circumstances. “This is the work of criminal alien smugglers who have no regard for human life,” said Del Rio Sector Chief Patrol Agent Anthony “Scott” Good. “Doors on freight cars are locked externally, and migrants are trapped for an indefinite amount of time without food or water. No one should believe the lies of smugglers who say they can provide safety because they only care about the money they can gain by exploiting vulnerable people.” Under the leadership of President Donald J. Trump and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, the dedicated men and women of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, alongside our law enforcement partners, have worked tirelessly to make our communities safer. title: CBP protects U.S. agriculture with first-in-nation pathogen interception at George Bush Intercontinental Airport
body: HOUSTON — U.S. Customs and Border Protection agriculture specialists at George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) recently intercepted a plant pathogen never before detected at a U.S. port of entry. During an inspection of baggage belonging to a traveler from New Zealand, CBP agriculture specialists discovered eucalyptus leaves that exhibited signs of a suspected plant disease. Recognizing the potential risk to U.S. agriculture, CBP agriculture specialists intercepted the items and forwarded samples to the U.S. Department of Agriculture plant pathologists for further analysis. The USDA laboratory confirmed the pathogen as Davisoniella eucalypti (Mycosphaerellaceae). This detection marks the first time this specific pathogen has been intercepted in the United States. Davisoniella eucalypti is a fungal pathogen that poses a significant threat to Eucalyptus species. If introduced into the United States, the pathogen can cause severe defoliation and reduced growth rates, which would negatively impact the health of the trees and the economic viability of the timber and ornamental nursery industries. By intercepting this pathogen at the port of entry, CBP has prevented the potential establishment of a disease that could have necessitated long-term management and caused cumulative damage to U.S. forestry and agricultural interests. "This interception highlights the critical, frontline role our agriculture specialists play in safeguarding our nation’s agricultural resources and ecosystem," said Rod Hudson, CBP Houston Area Airports Port Director. "By identifying and stopping this pathogen at the port of entry, our CBP agriculture specialists prevented a potential threat from entering the country, demonstrating the effectiveness of our layered enforcement strategy." CBP agriculture specialists are the first line of defense in the protection of U.S. agriculture, forest, and livestock industries from the introduction of harmful pests and diseases. On a typical day, CBP inspects thousands of international passengers and cargo shipments to ensure compliance with federal regulations. The intercepted eucalyptus leaves were destroyed in accordance with USDA protocols to mitigate any risk of the pathogen spreading. Travelers can help safeguard American agriculture and natural resources by declaring all agricultural items to CBP personnel when entering the United States. Visit CBP.gov/travel to learn more. title: CBP Air and Marine Operations, U.S. Coast Guard Interdict Smuggling Vessel, Apprehend 23 Illegals
body: MIAMI — CBP Air and Marine Operations and the U.S. Coast Guard interdicted a smuggling vessel early Tuesday morning, resulting in the apprehension of 23 illegal aliens near Angelfish Creek, Florida. On Sept. 15, 2026, an Air and Marine Operations Multi-Role Enforcement Aircraft conducting an Operation Vigilant Sentry patrol detected a surface target of interest off the Florida coast. Marine Interdiction Agents from the Miami Marine Unit and Key Largo Marine Unit coordinated with the U.S. Coast Guard for a successful interdiction of the 27-foot cuddy cabin vessel without incident. The interdiction resulted in the apprehension of one suspected smuggler, a Cuban national, and 22 illegal aliens of various nationalities. The group included eight Ecuadorian nationals, 13 Chinese nationals, and one Dominican national. “Attempting to enter the United States illegally by sea is extremely dangerous and will not go undetected,” said Executive Director Andres Blanco, Southeast Region. “This interdiction demonstrates the strength of our maritime partnerships and our commitment to stopping human smuggling organizations before they can put more lives at risk. Those who attempt these dangerous voyages face arrest, prosecution, removal, and the very real possibility of losing their lives at sea.” The individuals were transferred to the U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Pablo Valent for processing. The vessel was seized by authorities. "The U.S. border remains secure due to highly capable teams and coordinated interagency enforcement,” said Lt. Corryn Ulrich, commanding officer of Pablo Valent. “We remain ready to save lives and enforce federal law at sea." CBP Air and Marine Operations safeguard the nation by anticipating and confronting security threats through aviation and maritime law enforcement expertise. The U.S. Coast Guard remains committed to maritime safety and security through interagency cooperation and enforcement of federal laws. Under the leadership of President Donald J. title: Del Rio Sector Border Patrol agents rescue four trapped in portable water tank
body: DEL RIO, Texas – Del Rio Sector Border Patrol agents rescued four illegal aliens trapped in a water tank in the back of a pickup truck. Four trapped in water tank. While patrolling a rural highway on the evening of Sept. 14, agents assigned to the Eagle Pass South Border Patrol Station encountered a 2007 Ford F150 pickup truck. Upon inspection, agents found four individuals trapped inside a small portable water tank in the bed of the pickup with no means of freeing themselves. Using power tools, agents were able to open the tank and extract the four. The individuals, two Bolivian nationals, one Cuban, and one Colombian declined medical attention and were transported to the Uvalde South Station for processing. 2007 Ford F150 pickup truck. The driver a 19-year-old male U.S. citizen was turned over to Homeland Security Investigations and faces a charge of 8 USC § 1324 (alien smuggling). “Smugglers don’t care for the safety of those they see as mere human cargo,” said Del Rio Sector Chief Patrol Agent Anthony “Scott” Good. “Putting people in confined spaces with no means of escape is dangerous and barbaric. title: Del Rio Sector Border Patrol agents arrest child sex offenders for illegal entry
body: DEL RIO, Texas – Del Rio Border Patrol agents separately arrested two illegal aliens, who were previously deported after being convicted of sex crimes against children. On Sept. 6, agents assigned to the Eagle Pass Station patrolling near the Rio Grande, encountered two individuals determined to be illegal aliens. Upon further investigation, one of the individuals, Johan Alexander Moncada-Narvaez, 40, a Venezuelan national, was found to be a convicted sex offender. Moncada-Narvaez was convicted in Minnesota of electronic communication describing sexual conduct with a child and engaging in prostitution with a minor. He was deported Aug. 7 after completing his sentence. As a convicted felon, Moncada-Narvaez faces a charge of 8 USC § 1326 (reentry after deportation), which carries a maximum sentence of up to 20 years in prison. On Sept. 9, agents assigned to the Eagle Pass South Station patrolling an area ranch, encountered two individuals determined to be illegal aliens. Upon further investigation, one of the individuals, Jose Enrique Vasquez-Nicolas, 31, a Mexican national, was determined to be a convicted sex offender. Vasquez-Nicolas was convicted in 2020 in Castro County of indecency with a child and sentenced to five years confinement. He was deported June 28, 2026, after completing his sentence. title: CBP, Puerto Rico police interdict human smuggling event near Culebra
body: FAJARDO, Puerto Rico- U.S. Customs and Border Protection Marine Interdiction agents and the Puerto Rico Police Department interdicted a suspected human smuggling event Tuesday near the island of Culebra, Puerto Rico. At approximately 6:30 a.m. on Sept. 15, an Air and Marine Operations asset notified the Fajardo Marine Unit of a vessel traveling from St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands, toward Culebra. Maritime interdiction agents from the Fajardo Marine Unit notified Puerto Rico Police Department officers in Culebra, who responded to the area where the vessel made landfall. Officers detained three individuals, identified as Indian nationals traveling as a family unit: one adult man, one adult woman and one juvenile. The Fajardo Marine Unit deployed two vessels to support the search and successfully intercepted the transporting vessel, which had one occupant aboard. Following interviews by Ramey Sector Border Patrol agents and agents from the Homeland Security Task Force Human Smuggling Unit, it was determined to charge the vessel operator, Kavon Wheatly, a British national from Tortola, British Virgin Islands, with a violation under 8 U.S.C. § 1324 for alien smuggling. The family unit will be processed in accordance with applicable immigration law and placed into removal proceedings. All individuals were transported to the Ramey Border Patrol Station for further processing. The vessel and 200-horsepower engine will be seized pursuant to 19 U.S.C. § 1595 and in accordance with agency regulations. “Human smugglers routinely place lives at risk for profit, using dangerous maritime routes and unsafe conditions,” said Christpher Hunter, Director of the Caribbean Air and Marine Branch. “This interdiction demonstrates the importance of coordinated operations among Air and Marine Operations, the U.S. Border Patrol, Puerto Rico Police Department and our federal partners.” Criminal charges are merely allegations. title: CBP announces construction of new Newton-Azrak vehicle maintenance facility
body: MURRIETA, Calif. — U.S. Customs and Border Protection hosted a press conference Friday, Sept. 18, to announce the construction of a new vehicle maintenance facility at the Newton-Azrak Station. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act funds the $28.7 million project, which will provide secure, permanent infrastructure to improve fleet maintenance, overnight storage and secure parking for the station's vehicles. The new facility will replace an outdated, rented off-site commercial garage that the station has used since fiscal 1997. "Among the most important tools our agents rely on every day are our vehicles," said San Diego Sector Chief Patrol Agent Justin De La Torre. "A vehicle that is not ready cannot support an agent in the field. That is why fleet readiness is mission readiness." Currently, the station's fleet maintenance operation services more than 92 vehicles, and mechanics service about five vehicles and one all-terrain vehicle each day. Because the current leased commercial garage is off-site and in disrepair, agents and mechanics must frequently transport vehicles away from the station. This logistical separation takes critical resources away from the active operational environment. The new vehicle maintenance facility will bring collocated maintenance, a fueling station, a vehicle wash rack, a vehicle vacuum, an impound lot, overnight storage and secure parking onto a single site. Additionally, the project includes essential upgrades to the station's electrical grid and a reinforced emergency power system to ensure the continuity of operations during power outages. "This new facility will provide our maintenance personnel with a purpose-built, on-site location that best supports their work and safety," De La Torre said. "We are not simply addressing an immediate maintenance need. We are creating permanent infrastructure that will serve the U.S. Border Patrol for decades to come." CBP's Office of Facilities and Asset Management is planning and executing the project. CBP awarded a $23 million design-build contract to the Haskell Company, using an existing U.S. Coast Guard indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract. Utilizing this existing federal contract allowed CBP to move to the award stage faster than a new standalone procurement would have permitted. The Newton-Azrak Station is named in honor of Border Patrol Inspectors Theodore L. Newton Jr. and George F. Azrak, who died in the line of duty in June 1967. The station's agents patrol the backroads and highways leading north from the border. Thanks to the Trump Administration’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, this facility–along with other much needed improvements and added infrastructure–will ensure continued success in securing our borders. title: Another first in Detroit: CBP intercepts giant scale insects never seen at a U.S. port of entry
body: ROMULUS, Mich. — U.S. Customs and Border Protection agriculture specialists at Detroit Metropolitan Airport intercepted a first-in-nation batch of potentially destructive giant scale insects earlier this year. Local CBP and U.S. Department of Agriculture officials tentatively identified the tiny pests as a type of giant scale in February. The USDA later confirmed on Aug. 7 that the insects belonged to the Aspidoproctus species. Records indicate this was the first time the species had been encountered at a U.S. port of entry. The approximately 5-mm-long insects—dark in color and covered by waxy, light-colored protrusions—were found feeding on the surface of fresh pine bark brought in for medicinal purposes during a routine baggage examination of a passenger in transit from Cameroon to Illinois. Local CBP and U.S. Department of Agriculture officials tentatively identified the tiny pests as a type of giant scale in February. The USDA later confirmed on Aug. 7 that the insects belonged to the Aspidoproctus species. Records indicate this was the first time the species had been encountered at a U.S. port of entry. The scales and bark were seized for further analysis, and the traveler—a citizen of Cameroon—was advised of applicable regulations and released without incident. “This encounter provided us with an opportunity to educate the traveling public of the dangers exotic plant matter poses to U.S. agriculture interests and showcases the diligence of our agriculture specialists in protecting the homeland,” said Director of Field Operations Marty C. Raybon. “There is no such thing as a small threat.” This African genus of scale includes some of the world’s largest, with some species growing nearly 1.5 inches long. Other sap-sucking pests of this kind feed on a variety of shrubs and trees and can cause costly damage. Female scales can lay more than 5,000 eggs, and their tiny nymphs can spread easily by wind. A heavy infestation can harm plant health and damage trees, shrubs and other vegetation. “Our agriculture specialists are on the frontline of protecting Michigan’s vital lumber industry,” said Port Director Fadia Pastilong. “This first-in-nation interception is significant because pests like this can threaten America’s natural resources and wreak havoc among our most important economic sectors.” Travelers can help safeguard American agriculture and our natural resources by declaring all agriculture items. title: Trump administration delivers 16 straight months of zero releases at the border
body: WASHINGTON — Today, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Customs and Border Protection announced 16 consecutive months of zero releases at the border, continuing the unprecedented trend of historically low border crossings. “Sixteen straight months of zero releases at the border proves that President Trump’s policies are working,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “Catch and release is over, consequences are back, and illegal crossings have fallen to historic lows. This is what a secure border looks like.” The sustained decline in illegal border crossings and apprehensions—now at levels not seen in over three decades—shows the profound impact of robust enforcement policies. With daily apprehensions down 94% from the previous administration, the border remains more secure than at any point in history. “Border security starts with knowing who and what is entering our country—and controlling it on behalf of the American people,” said CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott. “That means people who cross illegally are apprehended, detained and removed—not released into the United States. Our agents are enforcing that standard every day.” Below is a snapshot of August’s key figures. Full monthly reporting can be viewed on CBP’s Stats and Summaries webpage. Border enforcement at historic levels Illegal crossings in August remained historically low: U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions decreased in August The U.S. Border Patrol’s apprehensions along the southwest border in August (8,870) were 5% lower than July. Nationwide, the Border Patrol’s apprehensions in August (10,939) were 3% lower than last month. Southwest border apprehensions were 94% lower than under Biden The U.S. Border Patrol’s apprehensions along the southwest border in August were 94% lower than the monthly average of the Biden administration; 97% below the peak of the Biden administration (December 2023); and less than what was apprehended in 5 days in August 2024. Zero parole releases The U.S. Border Patrol released zero illegal aliens in August, compared with 10,186 released by the Border Patrol under the Biden administration along the southwest border in August 2024. Drug interdictions that save lives CBP remains on the frontline against drug smuggling, seizing dangerous narcotics before they reach American communities. Fiscal year drug seizures 73% higher than under Biden: CBP has seized 73% more drugs this fiscal year through August than it seized during the same period of FY 2024. Fiscal year drug seizures 61% higher than the last four years’ average: CBP has seized 61% more drugs this fiscal year than it seized on average during the last four years in this same period. Cocaine seizures up: Cocaine seizures increased 28% , with 6,724 pounds seized in August 2026. Fentanyl seizures continue: Fentanyl seizures remain high, with 773 pounds of fentanyl seized in August 2026. Significant precursor chemical seizure: CBP, in coordination with ICE, seized over 120,000 pounds of precursor chemicals used to make illicit drugs in August 2026. Trade and tariff enforcement CBP plays a central role in enforcing U.S. trade law and supporting economic security. $349 billion in imports processed in August 2026. $24.6 billion in duties identified for collection in August 2026. Agriculture stats/seizures – securing American agriculture In August, CBP agriculture specialists helped protect America’s agriculture, natural resources, and economic prosperity. CBP issued 5681 emergency action notifications for restricted and prohibited plant and animal products. CBP conducted 112,180 positive passenger inspections and issued 790 civil penalties and/or violations to the traveling public for failing to declare prohibited agriculture items. title: Second chance, historic mission: Rescue dog Chloe joins U.S. Border Patrol
body: BATON ROUGE, La. — Not long ago, Chloe was running the streets of Deming, New Mexico, searching for safety and a second chance. Today, she is making a real-life impact with the U.S. Border Patrol and beyond. On May 15, 2026, Chloe became the first rescue dog to graduate from the U.S. Border Patrol Canine Academy in El Paso, Texas, as a Critical Incident Response Canine. That same day, the U.S. Border Patrol delivered its first canine oath of office to Chloe. She was sworn in by Stephen D. Crump, Director, USBP Canine Academy. "Chloe" a rescue from the Animal Rescue League of El Paso now serves as a Critical Incident Response K9 for USBP Chloe is assigned to U.S. Border Patrol Agent Miguel Carrillo at the Baton Rouge station. Since her first day on the job, she and Carrillo have deployed across the Gulf Coast region in support of U.S. Customs and Border Protection employees, their families and partner public safety agencies. “Chloe’s story reflects the very best of service, resilience and compassion,” said Adam Calderon, acting chief patrol agent U.S. Border Patrol New Orleans Sector. “From being rescued in New Mexico to becoming the first rescue dog to graduate from the U.S. Border Patrol Canine Academy as a Critical Incident Response Canine, Chloe represents the power of second chances." Chloe came to the Animal Rescue League of El Paso from a high-kill shelter in New Mexico. She was taken in by the Deming County Humane Society on Jan. 29, 2026, and was placed on the euthanasia list less than two weeks later. The Animal Rescue League of El Paso pulled Chloe from the shelter and brought her to its facility on Feb. 10, 2026. (l-r) Border Patrol Agent Miguel Carrillo, Lety Medrano, and Loretta Hyde of the Animal Rescue League of El Paso at Chloe’s swearing in ceremony, Border Patrol Canine Academy, in El Paso, TX. Loretta Hyde, founder of the Animal Rescue League of El Paso, quickly recognized Chloe’s abilities and potential. Chloe was later selected to enter the Customs and Border Protection canine program. “Chloe’s journey is a powerful reminder that with patience, purpose and a second chance, extraordinary things are possible,” said Miguel Carrillo, U.S. Border Patrol agent, and Chloe’s handler. “She is serving those who serve our nation, and her work is already making a meaningful difference.” The Border Patrol Critical Incident Response Canine Handler Course is a five-week certification course held at the Border Patrol Canine Academy in El Paso. The course includes basic obedience, critical incident response training and deployment preparation with the assigned canine and handler. The U.S. Border Patrol established the Support Canine Program, now known as the Critical Incident Response Canine Program, after the May 24, 2022, mass shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, where 21 people were killed. Then-U.S. Border Patrol Chief Raul Ortiz recognized the need for additional support for employees exposed to trauma and insisted on the program’s creation. The mission of the Critical Incident Response Canine Program is to help reduce stress, anxiety and depression, lessen the effects of trauma after critical incidents, improve staff morale and assist employees and families as they process grief and loss. A Critical Incident Response Canine is certified for approved field deployments to provide support to agents, staff and families during critical incidents and crisis events. The program is supported by chaplains and peer support members. In her role, Chloe provides comfort and emotional support to agents, employees and families during critical incidents, times of grief and high-stress operations. Chloe’s impact extends beyond CBP. Following the line-of-duty death of Deputy U.S. Marshal Drew Hanson, who was shot and killed July 13, 2026, while serving an arrest warrant for a fugitive in Alexandria, Louisiana. Chloe and agent Carrillo attended services for Marshal Hanson. There, they provided comfort to his wife, children, parents, colleagues and other loved ones. Chloe visits area hospitals, providing comfort to patients recovering from illnesses. Chloe has also visited area hospitals, providing comfort to patients recovering from severe illness and to those receiving hospice care. Together, Carrillo and Chloe are a calm and supportive team. When Carrillo tells Chloe to “go say hi,” she happily engages those in need with affection and warmth, helping open the door for personal communication, connection, and support. From the streets of Deming to serving those who serve the nation, Chloe is proof that rescue dogs do more than survive. They inspire, heal, and change lives. Learn more at www.CBP.gov . title: CBP hosts Trade and Cargo Security Summit in Dallas
body: DALLAS —U.S. Customs and Border Protection hosted the 2026 Trade and Cargo Security Summit in Dallas, Texas Sept. 8-10. This year’s theme, “Knowing Your Supply Chain to Remain Compliant and Mitigate Risk,” emphasized the shared responsibility of government and industry to strengthen supply chain security, support lawful trade, and protect the U.S. economy. “Every day we're protecting the homeland,” said Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “No way we can take our eye off our mission. And by the way, there’s no way we can do it without our partners who are in this room — your partnership with making sure that we have the technology, that we have the supplies, that we have the infrastructure coming in, that we have the supply chains working correctly.” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin delivered the keynote address at the Trade and Cargo Security Summit on September 9, 2026, in Dallas, Texas. With 1,300 in-person and 3,000 virtual participants, the Summit, also known as TCSS 2026, brought together importers, exporters, carriers, brokers, attorneys, trade associations, other government agencies, Congress, and the press for discussions with CBP leadership on the agency’s top priorities, policies, and initiatives. During a fireside chat with Executive Director Christopher Siepmann, of CBP’s Office of Trade Relations, CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott touched on several topics during the chat from the essential human role CBP plays in the emerging AI landscape; the link between economic, border, and national security; and CBP’s commitment to essential values when it comes to forced labor enforcement. “The economic security of this country is super important,” said Commissioner Scott. “But, our core values, sticking to our beliefs, and making sure that we actually stand for human rights — is just as important.” Trade enforcement was central to the Summit’s panels, breakout sessions, keynote addresses, workshops, and listening sessions. Attendees heard from CBP leaders on the importance of identifying supply chain and cargo risks earlier, and fostering partnerships that enable faster, smarter targeting while keeping lawful commerce moving. CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott and Office of Trade Relations Executive Director Christopher Siepman conducted a fireside chat on September 8, 2026, at the Trade and Cargo Security Summit in Dallas, Texas. CBP Deputy Commissioner Ron Vitiello, who opened the event, discussed critical trade topics including the Strengthening Customs Enforcement Executive Order, illegal transshipment, forced labor enforcement, ACE modernization, Enforce and Protect Act investigations and supply chain security. “Both CBP and the trade community have critical roles to play to ensure the economic security, national security, and prosperity of the United States,” Vitiello said. “That's why we're here: to strengthen supply chain security and safeguard the integrity of U.S. markets.” CBP Deputy Commissioner Ronald D. Vitiello delivered the opening remarks on September 8, 2026, at the Trade and Cargo Security Summit in Dallas, Texas. CBP senior leaders also reinforced the importance of understanding the full supply chain during the leadership town hall. “Do your due diligence now. It’s everybody’s responsibility in the supply chain,” said Executive Assistant Commissioner Susan S. Thomas, of CBP’s Office of trade. “Each entity must own its compliance. For example, an importer should not rely solely on a broker or freight forwarder to validate its supply chain.” This year’s Summit included opportunities for the trade community to provide direct input to CBP experts. In line with this goal, CBP encouraged attendees to provide formal comments on the Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking titled “Heightened Import Disclosures for Supply Chain Visibility.” “We prioritized mutual communication between the trade community and CBP by adding three listening sessions about the Strengthening Customs Enforcement Executive Order to the agenda this year,” Siepmann said. “Feedback from the trade community is important to us as we forge the way ahead.” Acting Executive Director of Office of Field Operations Cargo, Conveyance, and Security Salvatore Ingrassia moderated the Leadership Town Hall on September 8, 2026 at the Trade and Cargo Security Summit in Dallas with Office of Trade Executive Assistant Commissioner Susan S. Thomas; (not pictured) Enterprise Services Acting Executive Assistant Commissioner Diane Sahakian; and OFO Director of Houston Field Operations Jason W. Murdock II. In addition to the exhibits, demos, and sessions, TCSS 2026 provided attendees with other unique benefits such as Global Entry interviews for applicants in conditional status , 45-minute one-on-one appointments with the ACE Help Desk, in person help from the Customs Trade Partnership Against Terrorism portal team, and continuing education credits for customs brokers. This year, the Summit also featured a competition during the Supply Chain Traceability Brainstorming Session. “Participating teams developed recommendations on programs, technology, tools, and other solutions to help CBP improve visibility into upstream supply chains,” said Acting Executive Director Salvatore Ingrassia, CBP’s OFO Cargo, Conveyance, and Security. “The Summit provided a rare opportunity to engage with the trade community to hear novel ideas that could potentially help solve real challenges.” CBP publishes TCSS updates and information about past events on the CBP TCSS webpage. title: Philadelphia CBP agriculture specialists intercept rare Chief Goliath beetles being smuggled to Germany
body: PHILADELPHIA – U.S. Customs and Border Protection agriculture specialists seized three live Chief Goliath beetles on Aug. 19 in Philadelphia that were being shipped in air cargo from North Carolina to Germany. One of three live, rare Chief Goliath beetles being smuggled from North Carolina to Germany. CBP officers inspected an outbound parcel on Aug. 18 manifested as “4x play toy.” Instead, officers discovered that the parcel contained three large live beetles, a container with beetle parts, and two shadow boxes used to display insect specimens. CBP officers submitted the live beetles and photos of the beetle parts to entomologists with the U.S. Department of Agriculture Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service. The entomologists identified the three live beetles as female Chief Goliath beetles ( Goliathus cacicus (Olivier, 1789)), and the dead beetles as three stag beetles ( Dorcus sp , Family: Lucanidae). Chief Goliath beetles are native to rainforests in Africa. Researchers consider Chief Goliath beetles to be increasingly rare in the wild due to deforestation and agriculture expansion in the tropical regions of Africa, and overharvesting for the international pet trade. Exotic insects are highly popular among collectors and insect enthusiasts and are illegally sold through underground markets CBP officers submitted the findings to U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service wildlife inspectors who requested that CBP seize the shipment as smuggled wildlife. Live beetles are considered wildlife and require USFWS permits to import or export. “The illegal trade of exotic pets brings hefty profits for those willing to risk destroying a wildlife species and violating U.S. laws and regulations. Customs and Border Protection agriculture specialists remain committed to intercepting these smuggling attempts and working with our conservation law enforcement partners at U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to hunt down and hold smugglers accountable,” said Elliot N. Ortiz, CBP’s acting area port director in Philadelphia. The shipment consisted of three live and three dead beetles. USFWS is investigating potential violations of the Endangered Species and Lacey Acts. The live beetles were turned over to USDA. The remainder of the shipment was turned over to USFWS. USFWS is investigating potential violations of the Endangered Species Act and the Lacey Act for failure to declare commercial export of wildlife and trading in wildlife without a license. title: CBP air crews, Border Patrol agents arrest scout near Ajo
body: AJO, Ariz. — On Sept. 4, U.S. Customs and Border Protection Air and Marine Operations crews and Tucson Sector Border Patrol agents arrested an active scout during a coordinated enforcement operation near Ajo, Arizona. title: U.S. Border Patrol agents rescue three locked in rail car
body: Second recent incident at same location DEL RIO, Texas – For the second time in recent weeks, Del Rio Sector Border Patrol agents rescued illegal aliens who had been locked inside a freight car by smugglers. Agents discovered three individuals locked inside a freight car. On the afternoon of Sept. 7, agents assigned to the Uvalde Border Patrol Station were inspecting a stationary freight train on a rail siding near Knippa when a Border Patrol canine alerted to an autorack car carrying automobiles. Agents inspected the freight car and discovered three individuals locked inside with no means of freeing themselves. The individuals, one Mexican national, and one Nicaraguan, and one Honduran, were found concealed in the beds of pickup trucks in the locked rail car. They were transported to the Uvalde Station for processing. On Aug. 30, Uvalde Station agents rescued a group of eight from a locked autorack freight car on the same rail siding. “Attempts to make illegal entry via trains have historically had tragic results,” said Del Rio Sector Chief Patrol Agent Anthony “Scott” Good. “This is the second time in two weeks our agents have rescued smuggled humans locked in a rail car at this location. “U.S. Border Patrol urges anyone considering such rash action to understand their decision could result in disaster.” Under the leadership of President Donald J. title: Laredo Sector Border Patrol agents answer the call during Labor Day weekend emergencies in South Texas
body: FREER, Texas — As families traveled across South Texas during Labor Day weekend, help came from public servants trained to respond when lives are at risk: U.S. Border Patrol agents. Between Sept. 6 and Sept. 8, agents and on-duty emergency medical technicians assigned to the Freer Border Patrol Station assisted in three separate incidents involving medical distress and vehicle rollovers in the Freer area. None of the incidents were immigration related. Each response reflected the same commitment to protecting life, assisting the public and standing ready when seconds matter. In the early morning hours of Sept. 6, a family traveling through the Freer Border Patrol Checkpoint requested medical assistance for a child experiencing symptoms consistent with a panic attack. A Border Patrol emergency medical technician evaluated the child, checked vital signs, administered oxygen with parental consent and offered additional emergency medical support. After receiving care, the child reported feeling better, and the family continued their travel without further incident. The following day, local law enforcement requested Border Patrol assistance after a single-vehicle rollover on Highway 44 near Freer. Agents and an on-duty emergency medical technician arrived at the scene, assessed the driver and passenger, monitored their condition and coordinated with emergency medical services for additional care. Both individuals were transported to a Laredo-area hospital for further evaluation. On Sept. 8, agents responded to a second rollover on Highway 44 near the Webb-Duval county line. Agents and an on-duty emergency medical technician evaluated the driver and stayed at the scene until state and local law enforcement partners arrived. The driver declined additional medical transport. During the two rollover responses, Border Patrol agents and emergency medical technicians were among the first responders on scene. Their early arrival allowed them to assess the individuals involved, monitor their condition and provide support until emergency medical services and law enforcement partners arrived. “I am proud of the emergency assistance Laredo Sector agents provided over the holiday weekend,” said Laredo Sector Chief Patrol Agent Desi D. De Leon. “Our Border Patrol agents fill a vital role in our national security and are often the closest first responders in the remote locations where we operate.” Across South Texas, U.S. Border Patrol agents often serve in remote areas where distance, terrain and limited emergency resources can turn minutes into life-or-death moments. Many are trained emergency medical technicians, allowing them to provide immediate care while working alongside local, county, state and federal partners during vehicle crashes, medical emergencies, natural disasters, and other calls for help from the communities they serve. title: Laredo Port of entry holds 25th anniversary 9/11 Memorial Ceremony at Juarez-Lincoln Bridge
body: LAREDO, Texas — U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Office of Field Operations, Laredo Port of Entry, held its annual 9/11 Memorial Ceremony to honor the victims, survivors, first responders and all those affected by the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. The ceremony took place during the early morning hours of Sept. 11 at the Juarez-Lincoln Bridge, where federal, state, county, and local law enforcement partners, along with first responders, gathered to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the attacks. “Today, as we stand united with our federal, state, county, and local law enforcement partners and first responders, we honor the memory of the lives lost on Sept. 11, 2001,” said Port Director Albert Flores, Laredo Port of Entry. “This commemoration reminds us of the resilience of our nation and the courage of the men and women who continue to protect our communities. Together, we reaffirm our commitment to never forget and to uphold the values of service and sacrifice that define us.” The ceremony featured a series of solemn tributes. The Laredo Fire Department led the procession with pipes and drums, while law enforcement agencies stood in formation. A combined Honor Guard presented the colors and raised the American flag, which was then lowered to half-staff in memory of the victims. A rifle team performed a three-volley salute, followed by the playing of “Taps” and a rendition of “Amazing Grace.” At precisely 7:46 a.m., marking the moment Flight 11 struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center, participants observed a moment of silence. CBP’s Air and Marine Operations also honored the occasion with a flyover above the port of entry, providing a moving visual tribute. Representatives from numerous agencies attended the ceremony, including CBP’s Office of Field Operations, U.S. Border Patrol, Air and Marine Operations, Office of Human Resources Management, Office of Trade and Customs-Trade Partnership Against Terrorism; Homeland Security Investigations; Transportation Security Administration; Laredo Fire Department; Laredo Police Department; Webb County Sheriff’s Office; Texas Department of Public Safety; and the U.S. Consulate General. The Laredo Port of Entry extends its deepest gratitude to all participating agencies and partners who helped make this solemn service possible. Their strength, bravery and unwavering dedication exemplify the highest ideals of public service. This commemoration serves not only as a tribute to the victims of Sept. 11, but also as a recognition of the steadfast commitment of law enforcement partners and first responders who continue to serve their communities with honor. title: U.S. Border Patrol Big Bend Sector remembers 9/11
body: Alpine, Texas For More Information Contact: Landon Hutchens (202) 407-4241; landon.r.hutchens@cbp.dhs.gov ALPINE, Texas – The U.S. Border Patrol Big Bend Sector held a commemoration ceremony to mark the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Today at the U.S. Border Patrol Station in Alpine, Texas the solemn remembrance ceremony included the lowering of the U.S. flag to half-staff as a tribute to the victims of the terrorist attacks, singing of the national anthem, a wreath laying ceremony, a fly over of CBP and Texas Department of Public Safety helicopters and an address by U.S. Border Patrol Big Bend Acting Sector Chief Patrol Agent Josh Barrett. Border Patrol agents, first responders, and community members gathered during the ceremony to pay tribute to the nearly 3,000 victims of the 2001 terrorist attacks. U.S. Border Patrol Agents from the Alpine, Texas Station remember the almost 3,000 American who lost their lives on September 11, 2001. The ceremony was centered around a 1,300-pound piece of steel from the World Trade Center—a powerful symbol of the nation’s resilience. This artifact, the only one of its kind in the Big Bend Sector, has been a focal point of reflection and remembrance since its arrival at the Alpine Station in 2012. Twisted and scarred by the events of September 11, 2001, the steel now anchors the station’s 9/11 memorial. The 9/11 artifact was brought to the Alpine Station through the dedicated efforts of former Border Patrol agents, local law enforcement officers, and the local community, who recognized the profound significance of securing a piece of history for the remote outpost. The team pursued the artifact with a commitment to ensuring that the sacrifices of Sept. 11, 2001, would not be forgotten in the Big Bend Sector. Their successful application to the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which oversees the distribution of World Trade Center artifacts, resulted in the delivery of the 1,300-pound piece of steel to Alpine, where it now serves as a powerful symbol of national resilience and remembrance. “This year marks 25 years since the September 11 terrorist attacks on our country. title: Norfolk CBP officers seize nearly $300k in automotive radiators and dehumidifiers imported through identity fraud
body: NORFOLK, Va. – U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers seized nearly $300,000 in imported dehumidifiers and automotive radiators in Norfolk on Aug. 25 that were imported using fraudulent identities. Officers seized 1,043 auto radiators imported using a stolen identity. CBP officers initially inspected both shipments in mid-August after they arrived from China. Officers detected discrepancies in the importation and identification documents and detained the shipments. Officers sought additional documentation and identification from the brokers. One shipment contained 1,043 automotive radiators with a declared value of $5,775 that were destined to an address in Cheyenne, Wyo. The other shipment contained 420 high-capacity 70-pint dehumidifiers with a declared value of $10,080 that were destined to an address in Artesia, Calif. Officers located and contacted both individuals identified as being the importers of record for each shipment. Each denied ordering the commercial goods or operating a business that imports commercial goods. Officers determined that both individuals were subjects of identity fraud. Officers also seized 420 high-capacity dehumidifiers imported using the stolen identity of another victim. CBP officers seized the radiators and dehumidifiers pursuant to 19 USC 1595a(c)(1)(A) for violation of 18 USC 542 for the entry of goods by means of false statements. Trade experts at CBP’s Center of Excellence and Expertise appraised the dehumidifiers at $181,847 and the automotive radiators at $110,176. Investigations into both shipments continue. “Legitimate businesses do not use the stolen identities of American citizens to import commercial goods,” CBP Area Port Director Keri Brady, Area Port of Norfolk-Newport News. “Customs and Border Protection officers will continue to combat transnational crime by detecting and intercepting illicit shipments imported by nefarious business operators and working with our law enforcement partners to hold them accountable.” Read more about CBP’s trade enforcement approach that helps to ensure a fair and competitive trade environment. title: CBP launches new trusted traveler mobile app
body: WASHINGTON — U.S. Customs and Border Protection has launched a new Trusted Traveler App mobile app to continue its mission to improve and innovate the traveler experience. “The new Trusted Traveler mobile app brings application and membership management features together with our popular Global Entry arrival confirmation feature,” said Executive Assistant Commissioner Diane J. Sabatino, of CBP’s Office of Field Operations. “Having one official app to support all of our services makes every step of the journey less complicated for travelers.” The Trusted Traveler App brings the capabilities of two previously available apps into one official app. The free app, available in both the Apple App Store and Google Play, helps travelers manage their applications to Global Entry, NEXUS, SENTRI, or FAST. It supports membership updates, enrollment interview scheduling, and the ability to renew memberships. The app also allows Global Entry members to confirm their international arrivals with CBP when arriving at a U.S. airport. Currently, 85 airports and multiple CBP Preclearance locations support the new Trusted Traveler App. Travelers who have used the previous Global Entry Mobile App and/or Trusted Traveler Programs App can download the new app and sign in using their existing credentials, and their profile and membership information will transfer over. The previously available apps have been discontinued. Global Entry, one of the Department of Homeland Security’s Trusted Traveler Programs, provides expedited clearance for prescreened, low-risk travelers upon arrival in the United States. All applicants undergo rigorous background checks and in-person interviews before enrollment. Global Entry has millions of members worldwide benefiting from expedited entry services each year. Through these partnerships, CBP continues to promote secure and efficient travel while fostering stronger multilateral relationships. title: Border Patrol Marine Unit rescues man struggling in Rio Grande
body: LAREDO, Texas — Laredo Sector Border Patrol agents assigned to the Laredo Sector Marine Unit rescued a man from the Rio Grande on Aug. 29, after he was seen struggling to stay afloat and repeatedly submerging during an attempted illegal crossing. At 7:30 a.m., agents assigned to the Laredo South Station observed the man in distress in the river. Agents reported that he went underwater for several seconds on multiple occasions and appeared unable to safely remain above the surface. Marine Unit agents responded aboard a U.S. Border Patrol vessel, reached the man and pulled him from the water. On-duty emergency medical technicians were contacted and evaluated him after the rescue. He was later turned over to agents assigned to the Laredo South Station. The rescue occurred after Marine Unit agents encountered multiple people attempting to enter the United States illegally. Six illegal aliens, including the man who was rescued, were taken into custody by Border Patrol agents and processed in accordance with applicable law and policy. “This rescue is a reminder of how dangerous the Rio Grande can be and how quickly an attempted crossing can become a life-threatening emergency,” said Desi De Leon, Laredo Sector Chief Patrol Agent. “Our agents have a duty to enforce the law and secure the border, but they also have a responsibility to protect human life. When someone is in distress, our agents act quickly.” The Rio Grande remains one of the most dangerous crossing areas along the Southwest border. Strong currents, shifting depths, fatigue and changing river conditions can overwhelm a person within seconds, even in areas that may appear calm from the surface. Transnational criminal organizations and human smugglers routinely exploit vulnerable people by encouraging them to attempt dangerous crossings while minimizing the risks. These organizations profit from desperation and often place migrants in hazardous situations with little regard for their safety. U.S. Border Patrol urges individuals not to risk their lives by attempting to cross the Rio Grande. The river is unpredictable, and smugglers cannot guarantee safe passage. title: Baltimore CBP officers seize $142k in clandestinely imported plywood from China
body: BALTIMORE – U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers seized a shipment of over 8,500 falcata plywood sheets in Baltimore on Aug. 27 that were imported using a stolen identity, were undervalued, and were clandestinely imported from China. CBP valued the shipment at $142,372. Officers seized over 8,500 falcata plywood sheets unlawfully transshipped from China. CBP officers initially inspected the shipment on July 9. The importer declared that the shipment was sourced from Indonesia and was valued at nearly $19,000. It was destined to an address near Denver. Officers detained the shipment for further investigation. CBP officers learned that the importer of record used a fraudulent identity on import documentation and tampered with the shipping invoice. The victim of the identity fraud confirmed that they did not order the plywood, and they were not associated with the importing company. Officers also determined that the plywood originated in China and was subject to antidumping and countervailing duties. Importing China-origin goods transshipped through third countries to evade anti-dumping and countervailing duty ( AD/CVD ) laws is illegal. CBP officers seized the falcata plywood as smuggled or clandestinely introduced merchandise [19 USC 1595a(c)(1)(A)]. An investigation continues. “Customs and Border Protection officers continue to crack down on illegal trade practices, such as commodities imported using stolen identities to mask the true importer, and transshipping misclassified and undervalued imports through third nations in a duty evasion scheme,” said Adam Rottman, CBP’s Area Port Director in Baltimore. “CBP remains committed to protecting our nation’s economic security, and American businesses and workers by combatting criminal enterprises that brazenly violate our nation’s trade laws.” Antidumping and countervailing duty laws level the playing field for U.S. companies by preventing foreign producers from flooding U.S. markets with goods sold below fair value or that are propped up by unfair subsidies. CBP officers conduct a robust trade enforcement approach to detect shipments that dodge antidumping and countervailing duties and third country transshipment practices that attempt to circumnavigate duty. title: CBP San Juan Field Office Emphasizes Maritime Reporting Compliance
body: SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico – The U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) San Juan Field Office, with jurisdiction over Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, is issuing a firm reminder to the boating community regarding mandatory requirements for reporting arrival into the United States. During this fiscal year, CBP has seized 3 vessels and issued multiple penalties across Puerto Rico to operators who failed to report their arrival as required by federal law. The mandatory reporting of arrival is a critical component of U.S. border security. These inspections allow CBP officers to verify the identity of all travelers, ensure that every alien entering the country is properly vetted, and prevent the facilitation of illegal immigration or the entry of prohibited items into the United States. Vessel operators are reminded that they must present all travelers for inspection at a CBP port of entry as required by law. The Reporting Offsite Arrival-Mobile (ROAM) application is a secure, mobile-based tool designed to streamline the reporting process for travelers entering the United States by small vessels. To use the program, travelers create a profile within the application, inputting their vessel and passenger information. Upon arrival, they submit their trip details to CBP. The application then provides a response: either an approval to proceed or a notification requiring the vessel and all travelers to report to a designated CBP port of entry for an in-person inspection. If the application is unavailable, operators must immediately report to the nearest CBP port of entry. Failure to report arrival is a violation of federal law under Title 19, United States Code, Section 1436. Violators face significant civil penalties, starting at $5,000 for the first offense and $10,000 for subsequent offenses. Furthermore, vessels used in the commission of these violations are subject to seizure and forfeiture by the federal government. Ignorance of these regulations does not exempt operators from enforcement actions. CBP has also seized multiple vessels and issued multiple penalties, in the U.S. Virgin Islands, due to vessel operators’ failure to report their arrival. “CBP is committed to ensuring the security of our maritime borders,” said the Acting Director of Field Operations for the San Juan Field Office, Efrain Rivas. “The ROAM program is a tool for facilitating legitimate travel, but it requires full cooperation. Failure to comply with reporting requirements carries severe consequences, including the assessment of penalties and the seizure of the vessel.” The boating community must review all reporting requirements by visiting the official CBP website or contacting their local port of entry. CBP remains dedicated to educating the public while maintaining the integrity of our borders through rigorous enforcement. title: Atlanta CBP officers stop more than 4,000 pounds of illegal Khat from entering the U.S.
body: ATLANTA — U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport have seized more than 4,000 pounds of khat since the beginning of the year, stopping the illegal drug from reaching communities in the United States. CBP officers inspect and seize a suitcase containing khat at Atlanta International Airport on Aug. 13, 2026 Khat, also known as Abyssinian tea or African salad, is a plant that contains cathinone, a Schedule I controlled substance under federal law. In four distinct enforcement actions this year, CBP officers in Atlanta intercepted khat in cargo shipments originating from India, the Netherlands, and Nigeria, as well as concealed in the suitcases of two U.S. citizens arriving on a flight from Paris. The khat seized by CBP officers at Atlanta International Airport will be destroyed. “CBP officers in Atlanta are on the front lines every day, identifying and intercepting illegal narcotics before they can reach communities across the United States,” said Pedro Ortiz, Acting Port Director for U.S. Customs and Border Protection Atlanta. “The seizure of more than 4,000 pounds of khat this year reflects the seriousness of this threat and the unwavering commitment of our officers to enforce federal law, disrupt illicit drug movement, and protect the American public from dangerous controlled substances.” Khat, also known as Abyssinian tea or African salad, is a plant that contains cathinone, a Schedule I controlled substance under federal law. The seized khat, with an estimated street value of approximately $500,000, will be destroyed. Nationwide, CBP officers and agents seized approximately 46,000 pounds of khat last fiscal year (Oct. 1, 2024, through Sept. 30, 2025) and seized nearly 19,000 pounds of khat during the first ten months of this fiscal year (Oct. 1, 2025, through July 31, 2026). According to the DEA, khat contains two central nervous system stimulants -- cathinone, which is classified as a Schedule I controlled substance, and cathine, a Schedule IV controlled substance. Cathinone is a stimulant that can pose serious health risks to users, including increased heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia, anxiety, agitation, and other harmful effects. Symptoms of khat toxicity include delusions, loss of appetite, difficulty breathing, and increased blood pressure and heart rate. The World Health Organization classified khat as a drug of abuse in 1980. body: DEL RIO, Texas – U.S. Border Patrol agents assigned to the Del Rio Sector rescued eight individuals locked inside a train car. Agents rescue eight from train. title: Over 13,000 prohibited agriculture items stopped in Chicago
body: CHICAGO– In early August, the U.S. Customs and Border Protection Port of Chicago Agriculture Cargo Unit intercepted a shipment containing live cacti, succulents, pork, plant cuttings, and peyote. The shipment, manifested as women’s nylon shirt, was intercepted, and after an intensive examination over multiple days, CBP seized 13,683 total pieces of prohibited plant and animal products lacking proper documentation, permits and phytosanitary certifications. Of note, agriculture specialists found four pounds of soil, one pound of seeds for propagation, and 22 pounds of pork. Additionally, a total of 31 pounds of peyote, which is a psychoactive controlled substance, was discovered and referred to CBP officers for enforcement action. This shipment originated from China, weighed over 1,700 pounds, and contained 68 prelabeled boxes. This is an example of a shipping method known as a “master carton” smuggling scheme, wherein a single shipment contains many smaller, unmanifested, individual shipments. These unmanifested shipments were prelabeled and would later be sent through a domestic parcel carrier to the intended recipient. “CBP’s Agriculture Specialists mitigate the threat of non-native pests, diseases, and contaminants entering the United States,” said Acting Director of Field Operations, Michael Pfeiffer, Chicago Field Office. “CBP agriculture specialists have extensive training and experience in the biological sciences and with agricultural inspections, inspecting tens of thousands of international passengers and cargo shipments at our air, land and sea ports of entry.” Live plants imported without proper documentation are prohibited from entry into the United States. Lawful live plant importation requires phytosanitary certification and must be imported through a United States Dept. of Agriculture Plant Inspection Station. Soil and compost prohibited from entry to prevent the entry of soil nematodes and other pests or diseases. title: CBP officers remove another 10 cruise ship crewmembers in Boston following Operation Tidal Wave investigation
body: BOSTON — U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers at the Port of Boston successfully removed 10 aliens from the cruise ship Norwegian Escape on August 31, 2026, as part of the ongoing "Operation Tidal Wave" initiative. This is the second such event in Boston within August, as the operation continues to target the possession and distribution of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and child sexual exploitation material (CSEM) among maritime crewmembers. On August 31, CBP officers encountered nine citizens of the Philippines and one citizen of Nepal aboard the Norwegian Escape. During secondary interviews, all 10 subjects admitted to previously consuming CSEM/CSAM. All 10 were processed for removal of conditional landing under Section 212(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) for crimes involving moral turpitude. “In just over two weeks, CBP has removed 24 cruise workers for possessing child sexual abuse and exploitation material, and we will not stop,” said Acting Director of Field Operations for CBP’s Boston Field Office Julio Caravia. “I want this message to be loud and clear: CBP will not tolerate anyone possessing this material entering the United States. Those individuals found engaging in this behavior will be arrested, removed, and face significant consequences.” In Boston, this operation follows the successful removal of 14 crewmembers from the Norwegian Breakaway, Holland Volendam, and Vision of the Seas throughout August. These efforts are part of a broader, nationwide initiative; previous phases of Operation Tidal Wave conducted earlier this year included Phase 1 in San Diego (April 2026), which resulted in administrative enforcement actions against 27 crewmembers from six vessels, and Phase 2 in San Juan (June/July 2026), which led to the removal of 14 crewmembers and the acceptance of federal prosecution for one individual. Operation Tidal Wave is a multi-agency initiative led by the CBP Office of Field Operations (OFO) Enforcement Operations Division, in coordination with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force. The operation aims to identify and initiate enforcement actions against cruise ship crewmembers who are associated with the possession, use, procurement, production, or distribution of CSEM and CSAM. The Area Port of Boston plans to continue this operational effort. This initiative demonstrates effective coordination among CBP field elements, targeting units, and HSI to address CSAM-related concerns within the cruise vessel crewmember population. CBP remains committed to working with domestic and international partners to identify and interdict those who pose a threat to public safety and to prevent the exploitation of children. Under federal law, any involvement with CSEM is strictly prohibited and carries severe penalties, including criminal prosecution, removal, and 10-year inadmissibility to the United States. title: Philadelphia CBP officers, K9 Nitro seize $19k in unreported currency from couple traveling to the Dominican Republic
body: PHILADELPHIA – U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers seized $19,000 in unreported currency after a CBP detector dog alerted to passengers boarding a flight to the Dominican Republic on Monday. Currency detector dog Nitro alerted to two travelers and CBP officers seized $19,000 in unreported currency. Nitro, a 3-year-old male chocolate Labrador retriever trained to identify bulk currency, alerted to two travelers attempting to separately board a flight to Santo Domingo, D.R. When asked how much currency they possessed, a 63-year-old woman declared $9,000 and a 79-year-old man declared $5,000. CBP officers escorted the pair to CBP’s inspection station. Despite initially claiming they were not traveling together, the pair possessed matching luggage and later admitted to traveling together. CBP officers discovered a total of $19,681. Officers remitted $681 to the couple for humanitarian purposes and seized the remaining $19,000. title: CBP supports federal response to New World screwworm threat
body: WASHINGTON — U.S. Customs and Border Protection, in coordination with the U.S. Department of Agriculture and other federal partners, is helping to eradicate the New World screwworm, a serious pest that, left untreated, can cause severe and even deadly harm to livestock, wildlife, pets, and, less commonly, people and birds. “CBP is committed to supporting USDA and our federal, state, local, and industry partners in preventing the spread of New World screwworm,” said Deputy Executive Director Suzette Kelly of CBP’s Agriculture Programs and Trade Liaison, Office of Field Operations. “By helping facilitate the timely movement of sterile flies, training frontline personnel, and sharing critical information, CBP is helping protect U.S. agriculture, animal health, and the broader economy.” Sterile flies are at the center of this federal fight. As of Aug. 16, USDA has confirmed 47 NWS cases, including 46 in Texas and one in New Mexico, with four active cases in three Texas counties. USDA’s Sterile Insect Technique program is working to stop the pest’s reproductive cycle by releasing large numbers of sterile flies into the affected areas. CBP’s role in the federal response also includes extensive personnel training, intelligence and information sharing, public awareness support, and clearing critical supplies and equipment needed for response operations. In addition, CBP helps ensure compliance with immigration laws for foreign nationals, such as pilots and mechanics, who may travel to the United States to support USDA’s NWS response efforts. CBP’s Office of Field Operations facilitated 96 shipments of sterile NWS pupae and viable NWS flies arriving from Panama through Del Rio International Airport, McAllen International Airport, George Bush Intercontinental Airport, and the Port of Pharr/Hidalgo. When sterile male flies mate with wild female flies, no offspring are produced, reducing the population over time and helping prevent the spread of the pest. CBP’s Office of Trade Relations also hosted an NWS awareness-level webinar July 26 highlighting USDA and CBP efforts to combat the NWS threat and provide stakeholders with important information about the federal response. Members of the public, livestock owners, and industry stakeholders are encouraged to remain vigilant and report suspected cases of New World screwworm to the appropriate animal health authorities. The second seizure occurred on Aug. 24, at the World Trade Bridge, when a CBP officer referred a 2007 T3 Freightliner tractor manifesting a shipment of “car parts” for a secondary enforcement inspection. Following a canine and nonintrusive inspection system examination, CBP officers discovered a total of 141.53 pounds of alleged cocaine within the trailer. The narcotics has a street value of $1,889,791. The narcotics combined had a street value of $2,967,148. CBP seized the narcotics and one trailer. Homeland Security Investigations special agents are investigating the seizures. Fulfilling President Donald J. title: CBP announces advance notice of proposed rulemaking to enhance supply chain visibility
body: WASHINGTON — U.S. Customs and Border Protection announced today that it has issued an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking titled “Heightened Import Disclosures for Supply Chain Visibility ,” designed to improve visibility into the supply chains of goods imported into the United States. The proposed effort will help CBP more effectively detect, stop, and prevent illicit imports that evade U.S. customs and trade laws. “Border security is national security. Knowing what is coming into this country is vital to our national security,” said CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott. “By strengthening visibility into the supply chains behind goods entering the United States, CBP can better identify high-risk shipments, stop illicit trade, and ensure that American businesses are not undercut by those who evade our customs laws.” This ANPRM supports the implementation of Executive Order 14411, Strengthening Customs Enforcement , which directs the Department of Homeland Security to strengthen enforcement of U.S. customs laws, increase transparency in international supply chains, and help prevent bad actors from exploiting outdated processes and enforcement gaps. CBP is seeking input from the trade community on potential ways to strengthen supply chain visibility for imported goods, including possible requirements to identify key parties in the importation process, improve business identifiers, collect or retain foreign export documentation, and use innovative supply chain tracing technologies. “Greater supply chain visibility is critical to CBP’s ability to detect and stop illegal trade activities,” said CBP Office of Trade Executive Assistant Commissioner Susan S. Thomas. “By seeking public comment, CBP is working to strengthen enforcement of U.S. customs and trade laws, while promoting a more secure and transparent global trade environment.” Public comments will help CBP assess considerations of these proposals as the agency works to improve enforcement, detect illicit trade and illegal transshipment, support legitimate commerce, and reduce unnecessary burdens, particularly for small businesses. “Supply chain visibility is essential to maintaining the integrity of our borders, protecting American businesses and consumers, and ensuring that legitimate trade continues to move efficiently through our ports”, said CBP Office of Field Operations Executive Assistant Commissioner Diane J. Sabatino. “By modernizing how we collect and analyze trade data, we are sharpening our ability to target high-risk shipments and interdict illicit goods—such as counterfeit items and dangerous substances—before they enter the country.” The public may submit comments through the Federal Rulemaking Portal at www.regulations.gov under docket number USCBP-2026-1058. Comments must be received on or before Dec. 1, 2026. These efforts support CBP’s broader work to modernize customs enforcement, protect American consumers and businesses, safeguard revenue, combat illicit trade, and strengthen the security and resilience of international supply chains. title: CBP announces 90-day extended hours program for empty trailers at Colombia Solidarity Bridge
body: LAREDO, Texas – U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s Port of Laredo, in coordination with Corporacion para el Desarrollo de la Zona Fronteriza de Nuevo Leon, will begin a 90-day program extending weekday operational hours for tractors and empty trailers at the Colombia Solidarity Bridge beginning Monday, September 14, 2026. Under the program, weekday operations for tractors and empty trailers will begin one hour earlier, at 7 a.m., and continue through midnight, Monday through Friday. The current weekday hours of operation are 8 a.m. to midnight. “This program reflects CBP’s continued commitment to facilitating lawful trade and improving the efficiency of cross-border operations,” said Port Director Albert Flores, Laredo Port of Entry. “By opening one hour earlier for tractors and empty trailers, we aim to help reduce morning congestion and support the transportation community that depends on efficient northbound processing at the Colombia Solidarity Bridge.” The program is intended to mitigate northbound morning traffic congestion from Colombia, Nuevo León, to Laredo, Texas. Data analysis indicates a significant volume of tractors and empty trailers transit during the early morning hours. Advancing the daily start time to 7 a.m. is expected to improve operational throughput and reduce wait times for transportation stakeholders. The extended hours apply exclusively to tractors and empty trailers. It does not apply to commercial conveyances transporting merchandise, including informal entries. Program Details: Effective Date: Monday, September 14 Duration: 90 days Current Weekday Hours: Monday through Friday, 8a.m. to midnight Revised Weekday Hours: Monday through Friday, 7 a.m. to midnight Applicable Traffic: Tractors and empty trailers only CBP remains committed to facilitating lawful trade while maintaining the security of the nation’s borders. For additional information regarding this program, stakeholders may contact Assistant Port Director Javier Vasquez at (956) 417-7801.
